items.stem: Unpack this Paper 2 question by explaining its command phrase and its key terms: "How do two works you have studied use a narrator's voice to shape the reader's sympathies?"
items.answer: "Narrator's voice" covers person, tone and reliability; "shape sympathies" asks how the reader is positioned.
items.markingKey: "Narrator's voice" covers person, tone and reliability; "shape sympathies" asks how the reader is positioned. Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a statement of intent and a comparative thesis.
items.answer: A comparative thesis makes an arguable claim about both works; a statement of intent merely announces what the essay will do ("I will compare...").
items.markingKey: A comparative thesis makes an arguable claim about both works; a statement of intent merely announces what the essay will do ("I will compare..."). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Write an arguable comparative thesis for the Paper 2 question: "Discuss how two works you have studied present the tension between public and private selves."
items.answer: Model thesis: Both plays expose the masks demanded by respectable society, but Wilde treats double lives ("Bunburying") as farce, while Ibsen treats Nora's performance as a tragedy that must be ended. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference.
items.markingKey: Model thesis: Both plays expose the masks demanded by respectable society, but Wilde treats double lives ("Bunburying") as farce, while Ibsen treats Nora's performance as a tragedy that must be ended. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference. Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem: Amara writes: "A thesis should be neutral so that the examiner does not disagree." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A thesis must be arguable; examiners reward a clear, supported position, not neutrality.
items.markingKey: A thesis must be arguable; examiners reward a clear, supported position, not neutrality. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "In what ways do two works you have studied explore the relationship between memory and truth?"
Write a comparative thesis statement that answers the question.
items.answer: Model thesis: Both works expose the gaps between remembered and actual truth, but Ishiguro uses Stevens's self-deceiving narration to make the reader detect what he suppresses, whereas Spiegelman frames Vladek's testimony with Art's present-day questioning so that the making of memory becomes the subject. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference.
items.markingKey: Model thesis: Both works expose the gaps between remembered and actual truth, but Ishiguro uses Stevens's self-deceiving narration to make the reader detect what he suppresses, whereas Spiegelman frames Vladek's testimony with Art's present-day questioning so that the making of memory becomes the subject. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference. Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "A complex thesis is always better than a simple one."
items.answer: The best thesis is clear first and nuanced second.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: complexity shows insight; nuance earns higher bands. Arguments against: complex theses can be unclear; clarity guides the essay. Supported judgement: The best thesis is clear first and nuanced second.

items.stem: Write three different comparative theses for one Paper 2-style question, then evaluate which is strongest and why.
items.answer: Indicative content: three arguable theses; evaluation by clarity, nuance and fit to question.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: three arguable theses; evaluation by clarity, nuance and fit to question.

items.stem: Which phrase best signals integrated comparison?
items.answer: "whereas"
items.markingKey: D. "Whereas" sets two works against each other.

items.stem: Distinguish between integrated comparison and block comparison.
items.answer: Integrated comparison discusses both works within each paragraph; block comparison discusses one work in full and then the other. Integrated comparison usually scores higher for criteria B and C.
items.markingKey: Integrated comparison discusses both works within each paragraph; block comparison discusses one work in full and then the other. items.stem: Explain why comparing authorial choices is better than comparing plots.
items.answer: Paper 2 assesses how meaning is created; comparing methods (e.g. narration versus stage directions) shows analysis rather than summary.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Paper 2 assesses how meaning is created; comparing methods (e.g. narration versus stage directions) shows analysis rather than summary. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Write a comparative paragraph for an essay answering: "How do two works you have studied explore the consequences of a single decision?" Analyse an authorial choice in each of two works.

items.stem: Plan the body of a comparative essay for: "Compare how two works you have studied present the role of women in a patriarchal society." Give three integrated comparative points.
items.answer: Example points: voice: Blanche silenced and removed versus Duffy's speakers taking the floor; tone: tragic versus comic and subversive; Stella's choice to stay versus the speakers' re-evaluation of their husbands. Evaluate whether either work offers escape from patriarchy or only critique.

items.stem: A student claims: "Comparing works means listing their similarities." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Comparison includes differences and evaluation of how each work's choices produce different effects.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "It is impossible to compare authorial choices across different literary forms."
items.answer: It is not only possible but productive: comparing how forms achieve similar functions is central to Paper 2.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: techniques differ (stage directions vs narration); effects are medium-specific. items.stem: Write two integrated comparative paragraphs comparing how two works you have studied present a central character's downfall.

items.stem: How many marks is criterion C worth in Paper 2?

items.stem: Explain the difference between a text-by-text structure and a point-by-point structure.
items.answer: A point-by-point structure discusses both works under each point; a text-by-text structure discusses one work then the other, often weakening comparison and balance.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the conclusion of a comparative essay should not introduce new works.

Supported judgement: It is usually the safest and most effective, but structure should serve the argument. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.
